approach: Use circumference over speed for the period, then work out the distance, the chord, and the velocity change over a quarter turn.

steps.text: The time period is the circumference divided by the constant speed.
From t = 0 to t = T/4 the particle covers a quarter of the circle, in a time of T/4.
Since the speed never changes, the average speed over any interval equals this constant speed.
The displacement is the straight chord joining the start and end points, which are 90° apart on the circle, so the average velocity is this chord divided by the time.
steps.equation: displacement = r√2 = 4√2 cm, average velocity = 4√2/(2π) ≈ 0.90 cm/s

steps.text: Over the quarter turn the velocity direction rotates by 90° while its magnitude stays at 1 cm/s, giving a velocity-vector change of v√2; the average acceleration is this change divided by the time.
steps.why_this_step: The velocity vectors at the two instants are perpendicular, so their difference has magnitude v√2, not zero.

final_answer.value: (a) T = 8π s ≈ 25.13 s. (b) average speed = 1 cm/s, average velocity ≈ 0.90 cm/s, average acceleration ≈ 0.23 cm/s²

common_mistakes.text: Subtracting the two speed values instead of the velocity vectors, 1 − 1 = 0, and concluding the average acceleration is zero, which ignores the change in direction.
Using the quarter-circle arc length as the displacement instead of the straight chord, which gives an average velocity equal to the average speed, 1 cm/s.
